analysis.one_liner: Requires a state license and registration for every handgun and handgun ammunition purchase, and tightens rules on gun dealers.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 1994 with one cosponsor, the bill sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a vote and died when that Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal to sell, give, or transfer a handgun or handgun ammunition to anyone without a valid state handgun license, which would require a background check, a safety course and test, and registration of each gun with the state. It would have limited buyers to one handgun per 30 days, raised federal dealer license fees sharply, allowed inspections of dealer records and premises, made dealers financially liable for knowingly selling guns to felons or minors that are later used in violent crimes, banned the private interstate transport of firearms, expanded the list of people barred from having guns (including people convicted of violent misdemeanors and people under protective orders), created a federal center to trace crime guns, and restricted certain armor-piercing bullets. It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in communities affected by handgun violence, since the bill aimed to keep guns away from convicted criminals, domestic abusers under court orders, and gun traffickers, and to help police trace guns used in crimes. States would also have received federal grants (up to $200 million) to build the required licensing and registration systems.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would bar any sale or transfer of a handgun or handgun ammunition to someone without a valid state handgun license, and would require each state's license system to include a fingerprint-based background check and a safety course and exam [S2][S3].

It would bar people convicted of violent misdemeanors and people subject to court protective orders from receiving or being given firearms or ammunition, closing gaps in the federal prohibition list [S2][S3].

It would create a National Firearms Tracing Center within the ATF to trace the chain of possession of guns and ammunition used in crimes, and would require dealers to help law enforcement trace guns [S2][S3].
It would let anyone physically injured in a violent crime committed with a gun a dealer knowingly sold to a felon or a minor sue that dealer for damages, including punitive damages [S2][S3].
It would require dealers to report stolen firearms by the next business day, secure their premises against theft, and face criminal penalties for stealing or dealing in stolen guns [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Handgun buyers and owners, who would need a state license, a safety certificate, and per-gun registration; gun dealers, who would face fees of up to $3,000 for three years, inspections, tracing and theft-reporting duties, and new liability; and states and the Treasury, which would administer the licensing, registration, and tracing systems.

drawbacks.text: The licensing-and-registration regime would be a heavy administrative lift: every state would have to build a new license and registration system meeting federal minimum standards, with federal grants authorized at $200 million for startup costs, and ongoing costs would fall on state law enforcement [S3].

Buyers would face new fees and waiting steps: a safety course and exam, license fees, and per-handgun registration fees that states could charge, and the one-handgun-per-30-days rule would apply even to law-abiding buyers making legitimate purchases [S3].

Dealer liability would apply 'without regard to fault or proof of defect' for sales the dealer knew or had reason to believe were to prohibited recipients, a strict standard gun dealers viewed as punishing them for crimes committed later by third parties [S3].

The ban on unlicensed interstate transport of firearms would restrict even private individuals moving their own guns across state lines, subject to a set of exceptions for inheritance, pre-existing ownership, and lawful transport [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill took the most expansive approach available to handgun regulation: universal licensing, registration, purchase limits, and dealer liability all at once. The public-safety case is strong on paper, but the design would have imposed real burdens on millions of lawful owners and thousands of small dealers, and states would have had to build entirely new administrative systems. Critics would also argue registration requirements raise civil-liberties concerns. As an introduced bill, it was never revised, amended, or tested in debate, so there was no chance for those design questions to be worked out.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late April 1994, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Bradley introduced the Handgun Control and Violence Prevention Act of 1994 on April 26, 1994 [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day; that was the last action ever taken on it [S5].
The bill attracted one cosponsor, a Democrat [S4].
The 103rd Congress ended January 3, 1995, and the bill was never reported out of committee or voted on by either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun dealers and manufacturers avoided higher license fees, warrantless record inspections, tracing duties, and strict liability for downstream crimes, and handgun buyers never had to obtain licenses, safety certificates, or registration.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun dealers, makers, and unlicensed buyers

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; its two sponsors were both Democrats, but no opposition votes were ever recorded [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have tripled dealer license fees to $3,000 for three years, required premises inspections, warrantless record checks, theft security, and strict liability for guns sold to felons or minors later used in crimes. Dealers would bear the administrative and legal burden of the entire licensing-and-registration system at the point of every sale.

Manufacturers would have to record ballistics data and serial numbers of handgun barrels, ammunition dealing would require a federal license, and new armor-piercing ammunition restrictions would narrow certain product lines. Reduced legal sales channels would shrink their customer base.

Carriers shipping firearms would have to verify recipients are licensed dealers and would be presumed to know a shipment violates the law if they fail to verify, adding compliance duties. The rules aim to stop illegal interstate gun shipments.
